hints: Think where the lobes point: one of these d orbitals points between the x and y axes, the other points mainly along the z axis with an extra ring.
walkthrough:
Picture what d orbitals look like**
Four of the five 3d orbitals look like a four leaf clover, four lobes. The $3d_{z^2}$ is the odd one out, it looks like a dumbbell along z with a doughnut ring around the middle.

Place the $3d_{xy}$ correctly**
The name tells you the plane. For $3d_{xy}$, draw four lobes in the xy plane, each lobe sitting halfway between the x and y axes, so the axes pass through the gaps between lobes. Nothing points along z.

Place the $3d_{z^2}$ correctly**
For $3d_{z^2}$, draw two large lobes pointing up and down along the z axis, plus a small torus ring centred on the origin lying in the xy plane.
Final answer: $3d_{xy}$: four equal lobes lying between the x and y axes in the xy plane. $3d_{z^2}$: two lobes along the z axis with a central torus (doughnut) in the xy plane.

hints: Start from the free $Ni^{2+}$ ion where all five 3d orbitals have the same energy, then think what ligands do to those energies in a complex.
Recall what happens when a d electron absorbs exactly the right amount of energy from white light.
Remember the colour you see is never the colour absorbed, it is the rest of the white light that is transmitted.
Compare the two ligands, $H_2O$ and $en$, and think why swapping them would change the energy absorbed.
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals**
In a free $Ni^{2+}$ ion the five 3d orbitals are degenerate, all the same energy. When six lone pairs from ligands approach to form an octahedral complex, they repel d electrons unevenly. Some d orbitals point straight at ligands and are pushed up in energy, others point between ligands and stay lower. This is d orbital splitting.

Absorb light to jump the gap**
$Ni^{2+}$ is $3d^8$, so there is space for an electron to move up. If a photon of visible light has energy $E = hf$ exactly equal to the gap $\Delta E$, a lower d electron absorbs it and is promoted to the upper set. This is a d-d transition.

Link absorbed to observed colour**
White light minus the absorbed wavelength is what reaches your eye. So if red light is absorbed you see green, if yellow-orange is absorbed you see blue. That is why we say the observed colour is complementary to the absorbed colour.

Explain why green versus blue**
$H_2O$ and $en$ are different ligands with different field strengths. They split the d orbitals by a different amount, so $\Delta E$ is different for $[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ and $[Ni(en)_3]^{2+}$. A different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency and wavelength is absorbed, so a different complementary colour is seen, green in one case and blue in the other.

Final answer: Ligands cause splitting of the 3d orbitals into two sets of different energy.
An electron is promoted from a lower to a higher 3d orbital by absorbing visible light.
The colour seen is the complementary colour to that absorbed.
$H_2O$ and $en$ cause a different $\Delta E$ so a different wavelength / frequency of light is absorbed, giving different colours.

hints: Count the donor atoms: three $en$ ligands each bind twice, so six N atoms octahedrally around Ni, picture them as a propeller with no plane of symmetry.
walkthrough:
Build the octahedron from chelates**
Each $en$, $H_2NCH_2CH_2NH_2$, uses its two N atoms to bite onto Ni, forming a five membered chelate ring. With three $en$ ligands you have $3 \times 2 = 6$ Ni-N bonds, octahedral. Draw Ni in the centre with one $en$ vertical and two $en$ roughly horizontal, using wedges or arcs to show depth.

Show chirality**
Arrange the three rings like blades of a propeller all twisting the same way, clockwise or anticlockwise. The mirror image twists the opposite way and cannot be superimposed. Drawing either twist correctly earns the mark.

Final answer: Octahedral Ni with three bidentate $en$ ligands in a propeller arrangement, one enantiomer (or its mirror image), e.g. all three $N-N$ chelate arcs drawn to show non-superimposable 3D structure.

hints: Use the coordination number of six to name the shape, and the pair of non-superimposable mirror images to name the stereoisomerism.
walkthrough:
Name shape and isomerism together**
Six donor atoms around Ni means octahedral geometry. Because $[Ni(en)_3]^{2+}$ exists as two non-superimposable mirror images with no plane of symmetry, the type is optical isomerism, the two forms are enantiomers.

Final answer: geometry: octahedral
stereoisomerism shown: optical isomerism

hints: Both cations are 2+, so focus on what differs between $Fe^{2+}$ and $Ni^{2+}$, think about ionic radius down the trend.
Link the more distorting cation to weakening of a bond inside the $CO_3^{2-}$ ion and easier release of $CO_2$.
walkthrough:
Compare the cations**
Both carbonates contain $M^{2+}$ with the same charge, so charge density is decided by size. $Fe^{2+}$ is slightly smaller than $Ni^{2+}$ in this context and so has higher charge density. Think of it as a more concentrated positive charge.

Polarise the carbonate**
A small, highly charging cation pulls electron density out of the carbonate ion and distorts it. This polarisation weakens one of the C-O bonds in $CO_3^{2-}$, making it easier to break to give $MO + CO_2$. Greater distortion means lower decomposition temperature, so $FeCO_3$ decomposes more easily than $NiCO_3$.

Final answer: $Fe^{2+}$ is smaller / has greater charge density than $Ni^{2+}$.
$Fe^{2+}$ polarises / distorts the $CO_3^{2-}$ ion more, weakening a C-O bond, so less heat is needed for decomposition.

hints: Think what colour the flask starts with from pale green $Fe^{2+}$, and what colour one extra drop of purple $MnO_4^-$ gives when no $Fe^{2+}$ is left.
walkthrough:
Spot the self indicator**
No indicator is added here because acidified $MnO_4^-$ is its own indicator. During the titration purple $MnO_4^-$ is instantly decolourised to almost colourless $Mn^{2+}$ while $Fe^{2+}$ remains. At the end-point the first excess drop of $MnO_4^-$ has nothing to react with, so the solution in the flask stays pale pink or purple. Starting from pale green $Fe^{2+}$ solution, you see pale green to pink.
Final answer: The colour changes from colourless / (pale) green to pink / purple (first permanent pink).

hints: Start with moles of $MnO_4^-$ in the $35.0 \text{ cm}^3$ titre using $n = cV$, then use the 1:5 ratio to get moles of $Fe^{2+}$ in that $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ sample.
Scale from the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ aliquot up to the full $100 \text{ cm}^3$ flask, then convert to mass of Fe and to a percentage of 2.62 g.
walkthrough:
Find moles of manganate in one titre**
Use $n = cV$ with volume in $\text{dm}^3$. $$n(MnO_4^-) = 0.0100 \text{ mol dm}^{-3} \times \frac{35.0}{1000} \text{ dm}^3 = 3.50 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

Use the equation ratio to get iron in the aliquot**
From $$5Fe^{2+} + MnO_4^- + 8H^+ \rightarrow 5Fe^{3+} + Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$$ one mole of $MnO_4^-$ oxidises five moles of $Fe^{2+}$. $$n(Fe^{2+} \text{ in } 25.0 \text{ cm}^3) = 5 \times 3.50 \times 10^{-4} = 1.75 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Scale to the original sample and find percentage**
The $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ sample is one quarter of the $100 \text{ cm}^3$ flask, so multiply by 4. $$n(Fe \text{ total}) = 1.75 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 = 7.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ $$m(Fe) = 7.00 \times 10^{-3} \times 55.8 = 0.3906 \text{ g}$$ $$\% Fe = \frac{0.3906}{2.62} \times 100 = 14.9\%$$

Final answer: moles $MnO_4^-$ in titre $= 0.0100 \times 0.0350 = 3.50 \times 10^{-4}$ mol
moles $Fe^{2+}$ in $25.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 5 \times 3.50 \times 10^{-4} = 1.75 \times 10^{-3}$ mol
moles $Fe^{2+}$ in $100 \text{ cm}^3 = 1.75 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 = 7.00 \times 10^{-3}$ mol
mass Fe $= 7.00 \times 10^{-3} \times 55.8 = 0.3906$ g
% Fe $= 0.3906 / 2.62 \times 100 = 14.9$ %
